keyVerseText: And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;
rootMeaning: The name רְעוּאֵל (Rᵉʻûwʼêl) derives from the Hebrew elements רְעוּ (Rᵉʻûw), meaning 'friend,' and אֵל (El), meaning 'God.' Thus, its root meaning is 'friend of God.' This literal sense enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing a relational aspect — not merely a name, but one that signifies a close, friendly connection with the divine. Understanding this etymology invites readers to see the bearer of the name as someone identified by a personal relationship with God.
usageInScripture: The word רְעוּאֵל appears 11 times in Scripture, predominantly translated as 'of Reuel' (6 occurrences) and 'Reuel' (3 occurrences), with minor variations like 'to Reuel' and 'of Raguel.' This consistent use as a proper name refers to several individuals: notably Moses' father-in-law, an Edomite descendant of Esau, a leader from the tribe of Gad, and a Benjamite ancestor. The range of bearers across different tribes and contexts highlights the name's widespread recognition and the importance of the relational identity it conveys.
theologicalSignificance: The meaning 'friend of God' embedded in רְעוּאֵל invites believers to reflect on the nature of a life marked by divine friendship and favor. Moses' father-in-law, also known as Jethro, exemplifies wisdom and alignment with God's purposes, underscoring how this friendship manifests in faithful leadership and counsel. The presence of this name among various tribes signals God's relational covenant extending across Israel's diverse people. For the Christian faith, it prefigures the intimate friendship with God made possible through Christ, encouraging believers to pursue a deep, personal relationship with Him as their true identity.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 36:4 states, 'And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;' introducing Reuel as a son of Esau. Here, the name signals more than genealogy; it marks a person whose identity is 'friend of God,' even within the Edomite lineage. This reminds readers that God's relational character extends beyond Israel, encompassing all peoples and promising friendship to those connected to Him. The verse grounds the name historically while inviting contemplation of God's inclusive relational reach.
